questionText: What is idempotency and which HTTP methods are idempotent?

target.learningOutcome: The learner can define idempotency by intended effect, list the methods that carry that guarantee, explain why responses may differ, and separate method semantics from an API-specific retry contract.
inScope: Idempotency versus safety and conditional updates
outOfScope: A claim that idempotent requests return identical responses
A claim that every POST using a header is automatically safe to retry

claims.statement: An idempotent method has the same intended effect on the server after multiple identical requests as it has after one such request.
GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent by standard method semantics, while PATCH is not idempotent by its method definition.
Idempotency applies to the intended effect requested by the user; separate attempts can be logged and a repeated request can produce a different response.
Idempotent methods can be repeated after a communication failure before the client reads the response because repeating the request has the same intended effect.

A method without an idempotency guarantee can be retried only when the client has another reliable way to know the operation is idempotent or was not applied. An API-specific operation key is one possible design, but request matching, key lifetime, completed-retry, and in-progress behavior remain application-defined.
claims.notes: RFC 9110 supports the retry boundary in the first sentence. The Idempotency-Key field and all lifecycle choices in the second sentence are explicitly presented as application-defined; RFC 9110 does not define that field.

claims.statement: Every safe method is idempotent, but PUT and DELETE are idempotent without being safe because they request application-state changes.
If-Match conditions an operation on the current entity tag to prevent an accidental overwrite; it addresses stale versions rather than identifying a duplicate logical operation.

examples.title: One logical payment request with an application idempotency key

validation.command: Parse the HTTP request and review the stated key-reuse rules as explicitly application-defined behavior
validation.expected: The request is valid HTTP and the lesson never presents Idempotency-Key as a guarantee supplied by POST or RFC 9110

notes: The general Idempotency-Key header is intentionally described as an API contract rather than an RFC 9110 method property.
The sequence diagram shows one illustrative application design, not a standardized header lifecycle or the only possible storage architecture.

review.notes: The method set, retry semantics, response boundary, and safety distinction were checked against RFC 9110; PATCH was checked against RFC 5789. Idempotency-key lifecycle choices are labelled as application-defined rather than RFC guarantees.
